design_detail: Double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled crossover trial with block randomization and counterbalanced order (registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04516902), University Hospital Basel: 24 healthy participants (12 women, 12 men) each had four sessions at least 10 days apart (13 h in hospital plus a 24-h follow-up visit): placebo; MDMA 100 mg; LSD 100 µg; and LSD 100 µg plus MDMA 100 mg taken at the same time. Primary outcome: the 5 Dimensions of Altered States of Consciousness scale (5D-ASC), rated 12 h after dosing. Also: visual analogue scales and the Adjective Mood Rating Scale repeatedly, Mystical Effects Questionnaires, effect duration from the visual analogue curves, blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature, pupil size and light reflex, the List of Complaints, plasma oxytocin, serum BDNF, and plasma LSD, MDMA and metabolites up to 24 h, plus guesses of the condition. Peak values analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests; pharmacokinetics by paired t-tests. Many statistics are in an online supplement that was not among the files read.
can_establish: That in 24 healthy volunteers in a hospital, taking MDMA 100 mg together with LSD 100 µg, compared with LSD alone in the same people, raised blood pressure, heart rate and pupil size more (to levels similar to MDMA alone), made the self-rated effects last about 1.5 h longer, raised LSD blood levels (peak about 10% higher, total exposure about 36% higher, half-life 3.9 to 5.2 h), lowered and delayed MDMA's own peak, and did not detectably change the kind or peak intensity of self-rated effects, at these doses with simultaneous intake.
cannot_establish: What happens at other doses, with other intake schedules or repeated doses, in crowded or hot settings, with dancing, alcohol or other drugs, in people with heart or psychiatric conditions, or in people taking medicines that block the same liver enzyme; that the combination carries no extra serotonin-toxicity or overheating risk (24 healthy people, one dose pair, a calm hospital room); or that its subjective effects are equivalent to LSD alone (no equivalence test).

sample.recruitment: Word of mouth or a pool of volunteers who had contacted the research group because they were interested in a psychedelic trial; paid for participation (p. 1841, Methods and materials › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 25–65; exclusions: pregnancy; personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder (semi-structured clinical interview by a trained psychologist); interfering medications (e.g. antidepressants, antipsychotics, sedatives); chronic or acute physical illness; smoking more than 10 cigarettes a day; lifetime use of hallucinogens or MDMA more than 20 times; illicit drug use in the last 2 months (cannabis excepted) or during the study (urine tests). Alcohol limited to 20 standard drinks a week and one drink on the day before sessions (p. 1841).
sample.demographics: 12 men and 12 women; mean age 30 (SD 7) years, range 25–54. Prior use: 12 had used a psychedelic (LSD 6 people, 1–3 times; psilocybin 9, 1–2 times; DMT 1; mescaline 1), 9 MDMA (1–13 times), 12 a stimulant (methylphenidate 5, amphetamine 3, cocaine 4), 1 2C-B, 1 ketamine; 4 had never used an illicit drug other than cannabis (p. 1841).
sample.attrition: Not reported as such; Table 1 gives N = 24 (pupil measures N = 23), and some pharmacokinetic parameters for MDMA alone are from 23 people (pp. 1843, 1846).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers interested in psychedelic research with limited drug experience (at most 20 lifetime uses of hallucinogens or MDMA) and no personal or family history of major psychiatric disorder. People who combine the two drugs at parties, often with more experience, other doses, other timing and other substances, are not represented.

exposure.measurement: Given in the laboratory, double-dummy: LSD base as an oral solution in units labelled 100 µg in 1 ml of 96% ethanol, analytically confirmed content 92.5 ± 1.89 µg (n = 10 samples); MDMA hydrochloride in opaque 25 mg capsules, confirmed content 25.40 ± 0.48 mg (n = 9); placebo solutions of ethanol only and capsules of mannitol (p. 1841, Study drugs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions, single oral doses at 9:00 after a standardized breakfast: placebo; MDMA 100 mg (four 25 mg capsules); LSD 100 µg; LSD 100 µg with MDMA 100 mg at the same time; at least 10 days between sessions (p. 1841). The authors note that only one dose of each drug and simultaneous intake were tested (p. 1844).
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drug use in the past 2 months (cannabis excepted) and during the study excluded by urine tests; alcohol limited; heavy smoking excluded (p. 1841).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Urine drug test at the start of each session; at least 10 days between sessions (p. 1841).

comparison.controls: Within-person: placebo, MDMA alone and LSD alone in the same 24 people.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (crossover; equal numbers of women and men).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person comparison; expectations and prior experience were not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: 5D-ASC (primary outcome, 12 h after dosing, retrospective peak); visual analogue scales 0.5 h before and at 18 time points to 24 h (e.g. any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, feeling high, fear, nausea, alteration of vision, sounds influence vision, alteration of sense of time, ego dissolution); Adjective Mood Rating Scale; States of Consciousness Questionnaire (MEQ43, MEQ30); onset, offset and duration of the any-drug-effect response (threshold 10% of each person's maximum); blood pressure, heart rate and tympanic temperature at baseline and 18 time points; pupil size and light reflex at baseline and six time points; List of Complaints before and 12 and 24 h after dosing; plasma oxytocin at 1.5, 3 and 6 h; serum BDNF to 24 h; plasma LSD, 2-oxo-3-hydroxy-LSD, MDMA, MDA and HMMA before dosing and at 17 time points to 24 h (p. 1841).
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated psychometric instruments and visual analogue scales; methods for the subjective measures are detailed in the unread supplement.
outcomes.operationalization: Peak (Emax or Emin) or peak change from baseline; adverse effects as List of Complaints totals for 0–12 h (acute) and 12–24 h (subacute); duration from the any-drug-effect curve.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey post hoc tests within each outcome; no correction across outcomes (26 rows in Table 1 alone, plus the 5D-ASC, MEQ and mood scales in the supplement).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind, double-dummy. Guesses: during and after LSD + MDMA sessions, 50% and 46% of participants thought they had LSD alone; during and after LSD-alone sessions, 25% and 38% thought they had the combination (p. 1844).

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes; Table 1 gives mean ± SEM and post hoc significance (F(3,69)). Placebo, MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA: any drug effect 5.3, 64, 90, 93% of maximum; bad drug effect 0.2, 6.4, 18, 14; fear 0.2, 2.3, 13, 8.2; nausea 1.0, 7.9, 25, 21; systolic blood pressure peak 124, 148, 137, 150 mmHg; diastolic 77, 89, 85, 90; heart rate 77, 95, 92, 100 beats/min; rate-pressure product 9290, 13698, 12385, 14678; body temperature 37.0, 37.3, 37.4, 37.5 °C; acute adverse-effect score 1.9, 8.6, 15, 15; subacute 12–24 h −0.2, 2.5, 3.1, 5.5; oxytocin peak change 6.0, 289, 60, 286 pg/mL. Any-drug-effect duration 9.9 h with the combination vs 8.4 h with LSD alone (p < 0.05). Pharmacokinetics (Table 2, geometric mean, 95% CI): LSD peak 1.9 (1.7–2.1) vs 2.1 (1.9–2.3) ng/mL (T = 2.09, p < 0.05); half-life 3.9 (3.5–4.4) vs 5.2 (4.6–5.9) h (T = 5.00, p < 0.001); AUC∞ 14 (12–17) vs 19 (16–22) ng·h/mL (T = 3.53, p < 0.01); MDMA peak 233 (215–252) alone vs 208 (189–228) ng/mL with LSD (p < 0.001); MDMA time to peak 2.8 vs 3.5 h (p < 0.01). Editors' calculation: LSD peak +10.5%, LSD AUC∞ +35.7%, LSD half-life +33.3%, MDMA peak −10.7%.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04516902 (p. 1841). The registry record was not read. The paper names the 5D-ASC as primary outcome, while the stated primary hypothesis concerns good drug effects, well-being, openness, trust, bad drug effects and anxiety (p. 1840).
analysis.selective_reporting: Statistics for the 5D-ASC, MEQ, mood scale, effect-time parameters, individual complaints, blinding and metabolite kinetics are in Supplementary Tables S1–S8 (not read). The effect of LSD on MDMA's kinetics (lower, later MDMA peak, Table 2) is not mentioned in the text or abstract.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Compared with LSD alone, the combination raised peak systolic blood pressure (150 vs 137 mmHg), diastolic pressure (90 vs 85), heart rate (100 vs 92 beats/min) and rate-pressure product, to levels close to MDMA alone; body temperature peaks did not differ (37.5 vs 37.4 °C). Self-rated effects were not significantly different from LSD alone in kind or peak but lasted about 1.5 h longer, LSD blood exposure rose by about a third and its half-life lengthened, acute adverse-effect scores were the same as with LSD alone, and no severe adverse events occurred in 24 healthy people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion that MDMA acted as a blocker of LSD's metabolism (p. 1846), and the statement that the two drugs interact pharmacokinetically and not pharmacodynamically (p. 1845), go beyond the data: the enzyme mechanism (CYP2D6 inhibition) is inferred from other studies and was not measured, and the larger blood-pressure and heart-rate rises with the combination are themselves an added effect of MDMA. The statement that there was no indication of greater serotonin toxicity (p. 1845) rests on 24 healthy people at one dose pair in a calm hospital room and cannot address rare events or other conditions. The discussion says nausea was similarly frequent with the combination and with either drug alone (p. 1845), while the results say acute nausea was more frequent with MDMA than with LSD (p. 1842) and Table 1 shows visual analogue nausea peaks significantly lower with MDMA (7.9) than with LSD (25) or the combination (21) (p. 1843). The effects on oxytocin are called additive (p. 1842), though the combination's peak change (286 pg/mL) equalled MDMA's alone (289). The abstract's safety conclusion, that MDMA did not improve LSD's safety profile, is supported.

timeline.event: Schechter (1998): in rats trained to recognise MDMA, a low MDMA dose given with LSD produced a full MDMA-like response (cited in the discussion; animal study; not read here)
This study: the first controlled study of combined MDMA and LSD in humans, according to the authors

replication.where_it_stands: The authors present this as the first controlled human study of the combination; it comes from one laboratory and no replication is cited.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation (grant no. 32003B_185111 to MEL), the University Hospital Basel, and Mind Medicine, Inc.; open access funding provided by University of Basel (p. 1847, Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: MEL is a consultant for Mind Medicine, Inc. The other authors declare no competing interests. Knowhow and data associated with this work and owned by the University Hospital Basel were licensed by Mind Medicine, Inc.; Mind Medicine, Inc., had no role in planning or conducting the present study or the present publication (pp. 1847–1848, Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: University Hospital Basel and University of Basel. A company that funded the study, licensed its data and knowhow and employs the senior author as a consultant is recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized crossover studies of the combination with more than one dose pair and intake schedule, in larger samples, measuring blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and LSD and MDMA levels, reporting adverse effects in the main paper, testing the proposed enzyme mechanism directly (for example by CYP2D6 genotype), and using pre-specified equivalence margins for subjective effects.

domains.note: Block randomization with counterbalanced order is stated; concealment of the sequence is not described.
At least 10 days between sessions, urine drug tests at each session.

Double-dummy; participants often confused LSD with the combination (half of combination sessions were taken for LSD alone), but placebo recognition is not reported in the main text and expectancy can shape self-ratings.
N = 24 throughout Table 1 (23 for pupil measures); degrees of freedom fit complete data.
Self-ratings by participants who may have known their condition; blood pressure, heart rate, temperature and drug levels are objective.

Registered (registry not checked); primary hypothesis outcomes differ from the named primary outcome; most subjective statistics in the supplement; LSD's effect on MDMA's kinetics not discussed; one F value inconsistent with its p value.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A registered, randomized, double-dummy crossover with complete data. Concerns: self-rated outcomes under imperfect blinding, a supplement holding most subjective statistics, and contradictory statements on nausea. The paper may be cited, for these doses with simultaneous intake in healthy volunteers, for the combination's larger rises in blood pressure and heart rate than LSD alone (similar to MDMA alone), its longer-lasting effects, higher LSD blood levels and longer LSD half-life, unchanged peak body temperature compared with LSD alone, acute adverse-effect scores equal to LSD alone, and the absence of a detectable change in the kind of self-rated effects. It may not be cited to say the combination is safe or free of serotonin-toxicity or overheating risk, for other doses, timings or party settings, or for the enzyme mechanism, which was inferred rather than measured.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 24 healthy volunteers (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30, range 25–54), half of whom had used a psychedelic and 9 MDMA before, each received placebo, MDMA 100 mg, LSD 100 µg and LSD 100 µg with MDMA 100 mg at the same time, in block-randomized counterbalanced order, double-blind and double-dummy, at least 10 days apart, in a calm hospital room with one investigator.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Study design; Participants; Study drugs; Study procedures

key_findings.finding: Doses as given: the LSD solution labelled 100 µg contained 92.5 ± 1.89 µg on analysis (n = 10 samples), and the 25 mg MDMA capsules 25.40 ± 0.48 mg (n = 9).

Self-rated effects: the combination did not differ significantly from LSD alone on any visual analogue scale, the 5D-ASC, the MEQ or the mood scale. Peak ratings (Table 1, % of maximum, mean ± SEM; LSD alone vs combination): any drug effect 90 ± 3.1 vs 93 ± 2.6; good drug effect 87 ± 3.6 vs 95 ± 1.9; bad drug effect 18 ± 3.5 vs 14 ± 4.1; fear 13 ± 4.1 vs 8.2 ± 2.3; ego dissolution 82 ± 6.2 vs 79 ± 6.2; all LSD vs combination comparisons not significant. Feeling high was similar for MDMA alone (59 ± 7.4), LSD alone (70 ± 7.3) and the combination (77 ± 6.7).
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective drug effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 1842); Table 1 (p. 1843)

key_findings.finding: Duration: any drug effect lasted on average 1.5 h longer after the combination (mean 9.9 h) than after LSD alone (mean 8.4 h; p < 0.05).

Heart and blood pressure (Table 1, peak values, mean ± SEM; placebo, MDMA, LSD, combination): systolic 124 ± 2.4, 148 ± 2.9, 137 ± 2.7 and 150 ± 2.9 mmHg (combination vs LSD p < 0.001; vs MDMA not significant); diastolic 77, 89, 85 and 90 mmHg (combination vs LSD p < 0.05); mean arterial 92, 107, 102 and 109 mmHg (p < 0.001); heart rate 77 ± 2.6, 95 ± 3.4, 92 ± 4.5 and 100 ± 3.6 beats/min (combination vs LSD p < 0.05; vs MDMA not significant); rate-pressure product 9290, 13698, 12385 and 14678 mmHg × bpm (combination vs LSD p < 0.001).

Body temperature peaks were 37.0 ± 0.05 (placebo), 37.3 ± 0.07 (MDMA), 37.4 ± 0.06 (LSD) and 37.5 ± 0.08 °C (combination): the combination did not differ from LSD alone and was higher than MDMA alone (p < 0.05). Pupil size was larger with the combination than with LSD alone (7.2 ± 0.1 vs 7.0 ± 0.2 mm, p < 0.05).

Adverse effects (List of Complaints, mean ± SEM; placebo, MDMA, LSD, combination): acute (0–12 h) scores 1.9 ± 1.1, 8.6 ± 1.8, 15 ± 1.9 and 15 ± 2.2 (combination vs LSD not significant; both above MDMA, p < 0.001); subacute (12–24 h) −0.2 ± 0.5, 2.5 ± 0.9, 3.1 ± 1.0 and 5.5 ± 1.4 (combination vs LSD not significant; vs MDMA p < 0.05). Headache, lack of energy, loss of appetite and dry mouth were reported similarly often with MDMA, LSD and the combination; no severe adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Results › Autonomic and adverse effects (p. 1842); Table 1, List of Complaints (p. 1843)

key_findings.finding: Nausea: visual analogue peaks were 1.0 (placebo), 7.9 ± 2.6 (MDMA), 25 ± 4.5 (LSD) and 21 ± 4.8 (combination), MDMA being lower than LSD (p < 0.001) and the combination (p < 0.05), with LSD and the combination not different; the results text, from the List of Complaints, says acute nausea was more frequent with MDMA than with LSD.
key_findings.locator: Results › Autonomic and adverse effects (p. 1842); Table 1, Nausea (p. 1843)
key_findings.note: The discussion (p. 1845) says nausea was similarly frequent in all three conditions; the three statements disagree (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Blood levels (Table 2, geometric mean, 95% CI): with MDMA, LSD's peak rose from 1.9 (1.7–2.1) to 2.1 (1.9–2.3) ng/mL (T = 2.09, p < 0.05), its half-life from 3.9 (3.5–4.4) to 5.2 (4.6–5.9) h (T = 5.00, p < 0.001) and its total exposure (AUC∞) from 14 (12–17) to 19 (16–22) ng·h/mL (T = 3.53, p < 0.01); apparent clearance fell from 6.9 to 5.3 L/h (p < 0.01). With LSD, MDMA's peak fell from 233 (215–252) to 208 (189–228) ng/mL (p < 0.001) and came later (2.8 vs 3.5 h, p < 0.01), with no change in its half-life (8.3 vs 8.2 h) or exposure (3083 vs 3068 ng·h/mL).
key_findings.locator: Results › Plasma drug concentrations (p. 1844, left column); Table 2 (p. 1846)
key_findings.note: The text and abstract mention only the change in LSD's kinetics. MDMA values for MDMA alone are partly from 23 people.

key_findings.finding: The authors attribute the higher LSD levels to inhibition of the liver enzyme CYP2D6 by MDMA (inferred from other studies, not measured here) and suggest that similar or larger rises in LSD levels could be expected in people taking antidepressants that inhibit CYP2D6 (they name fluoxetine, paroxetine, duloxetine and bupropion), an interaction they say needs study.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Mood over time: the combination tended, non-significantly, to raise happy, open, trust and well-being ratings early in the experience compared with LSD alone; well-being dropped at 6 h when the MDMA effect ended, and the authors note trend-level lower well-being and higher depression ratings on the mood scale towards the end of the LSD response with the combination, possibly a more negative mood from 5 to 12 h in some participants.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1844, right column, continuing on p. 1845, left column)
key_findings.note: Trends only; the data are in Supplementary Fig. S3 and Table S4 (not read).

key_findings.finding: Oxytocin: peak changes were 6.0 ± 5.3 (placebo), 289 ± 38 (MDMA), 60 ± 9.0 (LSD) and 286 ± 30 pg/mL (combination); BDNF did not change significantly in any condition (F(3,69) = 0.5).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on circulating oxytocin and BDNF (p. 1842); Table 1, Hormones and Markers (p. 1843)

key_findings.finding: Blinding: during and after LSD + MDMA sessions, 50% and 46% of participants thought they had received LSD alone; during and after LSD-alone sessions, 25% and 38% thought they had received the combination; at the end of the study 25% mistook each for the other.

reporting_issues.issue: Three statements on nausea disagree: the results say acute nausea (List of Complaints) was more frequent with MDMA than with LSD; Table 1 shows visual analogue nausea peaks significantly lower with MDMA (7.9) than with LSD (25) or the combination (21); the discussion says nausea was similarly frequent with the combination and with either drug alone.
reporting_issues.consequence: On the visual analogue scale nausea was stronger with LSD and the combination than with MDMA; how often it was reported on the List of Complaints cannot be checked without the unread Supplementary Table S6.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 shows that LSD lowered MDMA's peak concentration by about 11% (233 to 208 ng/mL, p < 0.001) and delayed it (2.8 to 3.5 h, p < 0.01), but the results text and abstract mention only the effect of MDMA on LSD's kinetics.
reporting_issues.consequence: The interaction runs both ways; the text gives an incomplete account.

reporting_issues.issue: For pupil size after light, Table 1 prints F(3,69) = 4.2 with p < 0.001; an F of 4.2 on 3 and 69 degrees of freedom gives p of about 0.009 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the F or the p value is misprinted; minor for the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: Effects on oxytocin are described as additive, but the combination's peak change (286 pg/mL) equalled MDMA's alone (289), less than the sum with LSD's (60); only the 3-h and 6-h values approach or exceed the sum.
reporting_issues.consequence: The additivity statement holds only at some time points.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction states a primary hypothesis about good drug effects, well-being, openness, trust, bad drug effects and anxiety, while the methods name the 5D-ASC as the primary outcome.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which outcome was primary for the hypothesis test is unclear; the registry record was not checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says body temperature rose less with MDMA alone than with LSD or the combination, but Table 1 shows MDMA alone differed significantly only from the combination (p < 0.05), not from LSD.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor overstatement; the temperature difference between the combination and LSD alone was not significant.
